name: Adilabad Gondi
confidence_why: Srinivas 2010, the only first-hand study of Adilabad Gondi prosody, says the language has no overt stress, whereas Steever 1998 (a sketch drawn from Subrahmanyam 1968, which is itself does not discuss stress) and Krishnamurti 2003 (a statement about Dravidian as a whole) report non-phonemic initial-syllable stress; since every source denies contrastive stress and Srinivas puts the head of the word on the initial syllable, the disagreement is whether a weak initial prominence counts as stress at all.

Ph.D. dissertation, School of Language Sciences, The English and Foreign Languages University, Hyderabad (supervisor K. G. Vijayakrishnan), December 2010. Open access: Shodhganga handle 10603/108956.

catalog_quote: In AG too, owing to lack of stress the evidence for foot construction has to be located elsewhere. ... Simply because AG does not have overt stress, we cannot say AG does not have feet. As noted earlier, other plausible motivations for footing have been discovered in other languages. ... Since AG does not have stress, it is difficult to determine if iterative construction of trochees proceeds left to right (e.g., Bangla) or right to left (e.g., Latin). I proposed in chapters 2 (section 2.2.3; p. 30) and 3 (section 3.1; p. 44) that in AG, which is a suffixing language like many Dravidian languages, the head foot is at the left-edge of the Prosodic Word. ... From the discussion in 4.2.2, it is clear that every syllable in AG is a foot because of Upward Inheritance. Because the language lacks overt stress marking, the coincidence of the syllable and the foot (to use a term from Alignment theory) must be interpreted as representing syllable timing. ... Experimental evidence is obviously required to verify my claim. ... (8) The Core Prosodic Structure of Simple Words in AG: (a) The left-most/initial syllable constitutes the head foot in the Prosodic Word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: According to the only first-hand phonological study of this dialect, Adilabad Gondi has no overt word stress; every syllable is bimoraic (a moraic trochee by itself) and the language is syllable-timed. Prosodic headedness is nevertheless at the left edge: the initial syllable is the head foot of the Prosodic Word (it alone licenses aspirates, /h/ codas, short vowels and geminates). Steever's handbook sketch of the same dialect instead reports non-phonemic stress on the initial syllable; so the catalog entry should read 'no contrastive stress; if any, initial'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress recognised); iterative footing direction said to be undeterminable in the absence of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Structural exceptions discussed: sub-minimal (light) initial syllables licensed as degenerate feet at the left edge; vowel length contrastive only in the initial syllable, non-initial vowels always long.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (nouns and verbs elicited in isolation and from Subrahmanyam's 1968 word list; fieldwork at Utnoor, Adilabad district, May 2010). The author treats the initial syllable as the head foot of a left-headed Prosodic Word on licensing grounds, but explicitly denies overt stress. Conflicts with Steever 1998: 274 (handbook sketch of the same Adilabad dialect, snippet only): 'Stress, which is non-phonemic, falls on the initial syllable of a word.' Both agree that any prominence is initial and non-contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Srinivas 2010 studied the Adilabad dialect at Utnoor (Adilabad district, then Andhra Pradesh, now Telangana) with Gond informants from a village c. 40 km from Utnoor, building on Subrahmanyam 1968's Utnoor/Adilabad dialect; this is utno1237 Adilabad Gondi (= Southern Gondi, ISO wsg; Glottolog dialects Nirmal, Rajura). Steever 1998's 'Gondi' chapter is likewise based on the Adilabad (and Koya) material of Subrahmanyam 1968 (p. 271). Williamson 1889 and the Shodhganga theses by Achar (Mandla/Balaghat/Betul), Andres (Muria), Pandey (Dandami Maria) and Natarajan (Abujhmaria) concern other Gondi languages and were not used.

new_statements.quote: The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each). The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A noninitial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants.

new_statements.relation_note: Same relation as Steever: it asserts non-phonemic initial stress across the family, whereas the existing statement (Srinivas 2010) says Adilabad Gondi has no (overt) stress. Both deny contrastive stress. It is a family-level typological claim, not a description of Adilabad Gondi specifically, so it carries less weight for this variety than Steever or Srinivas. The listed open copy (ERIC microfiche) contains only an abstract that mentions 'suprasegmental features' among ch. 2 topics; an archive.org search found no other open copy of the 2003 book.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide generalization: no Dravidian language has phonemic stress; loudness normally falls on the initial syllable whether it is short or long; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as such; the only non-initial prominence mentioned is that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (weight-related). Also p. 27: 'Short vowels in non-root syllables (in unaccented position) tend to be lost.'
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is hedged with 'Normally'. Gondi is not singled out.
new_statements.identity_note: Steever's 'Gondi' chapter states it is based on the Adilabad and Koya dialects of Adilabad District (Subrahmanyam 1968), i.e. this variety (utno1237 / Southern Gondi wsg). Krishnamurti's statement is about the Dravidian family as a whole and does not single out Gondi or any dialect. Srinivas 2010 is Adilabad Gondi (Utnoor).

readall_conflicts: Srinivas 2010 (the existing statement; full-text dissertation on Adilabad Gondi from 2010 Utnoor fieldwork) says 'AG does not have overt stress' and 'the language lacks overt stress marking', while Steever 1998 (Gondi chapter built on Subrahmanyam's 1968 Adilabad data; snippet only) says 'Stress, which is non-phonemic, falls on the initial syllable of a word' and Krishnamurti 2003 (family-wide, p. 27) says 'There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word'. The disagreement is one of category (no word stress vs fixed: initial syllable non-contrastive stress), not of placement: all three deny contrastive stress, and Srinivas's left-headed prosodic word puts the head on the initial syllable, so no source places prominence anywhere but the first syllable. Subrahmanyam 1968 (already held by the project) is silent on stress. Steever 1998 p. 274 (snippet, fully visible sentence) says Gondi stress is non-phonemic and word-initial (fixed: initial syllable), and Krishnamurti 2003 p. 27 says the same for Dravidian generally; the catalog record codes Adilabad Gondi as no-word-stress from Srinivas 2010, who writes that AG 'does not have overt stress' while positing a left-headed prosodic word. The disagreement is type (non-contrastive initial stress vs no word stress), not placement; all sources agree stress is not contrastive. No fuller copy of Steever's chapter could be opened to see whether he qualifies…
